Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Check this draft for consistency with the index and world rules. Pay particular attention to whether every clue used in the scene is both introduced in the index and present in the scene's 'present' list; flag any missing provenance mentions. Check for any craft issues that would block (e.g. scene is all telling, no development). Return the audit file path and a short verdict (approve or list findings). Note: the draft referenced gaps identified by the builder — ensure the writer treated those as unknowns rather than inventing them.

That is in addition to your standing instructions above, not instead of them.
If it states a story fact that is not in your packet — a name, a measurement, a
quotation, a piece of history — that fact has not been checked against the index by
anyone. Ask about it or establish it yourself in the state delta. Do not write it down
as though it were already true.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No supernatural solutions or unexplained actions; the locked-room must be resolved by physical mechanism, misdirection, or human action consistent with the environment.
- All clues relied on in the solution must be introduced to the reader (or the narrator) before the reveal scene and have identifiable provenance.
- Times, locations and physical traces must be internally consistent (the watch's stopped time, hatch abrasions, ladder marks, oil stains and filing nick must align with the clockwork reconstruction).
- Forensic detail may be stylised but must not violate basic plausibility (no instantaneous chemical transformations, no impossible mechanical feats).
- The narrator (Aldo) is a competent, essentially reliable detective; he may withhold interpretation but not facts.
- No later scene may introduce new characters, locations, or significant objects not listed above without explicitly adding them to the index with provenance.

## The draft

People had gathered before I stepped over the threshold: a pair of uniforms doing their polite, slow circuit, Henry Crane standing as if he were a model of restraint, Marta planted like a hinge beside the desk, Derek from next door lingering in the hall with the careful stillness of a man who watches mechanisms, and Inspector Rao keeping to the edge with his notebook closed but ready.

The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill showed a faint dusting of garden pollen. Light lay across the floorboards in a flat, indifferent pool. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. A small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three short, rough-ended butts of a coarse tobacco I did not recognise from the household's usual brand. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like a lathe left running and then abandoned. It sat in the room as insistently as any witness.

Those are the things the room offers first: how it was closed, what was in a body's hold, what time a stopped instrument insists upon. But there were other absences I noticed at once. I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I made notes. Photographing and cataloguing are someone else's ordinance; deduction is mine. A locked room is a contract that begins with a set of physical sentences and leaves you to supply the connecting verbs. I closed my notebook on that edge and let the room keep its silence a little longer—waiting is part of listening.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

People had gathered before I stepped over the threshold: a pair of uniforms doing their polite, slow circuit, Henry Crane standing as if he were a model of restraint, Marta planted like a hinge beside the desk, Derek from next door lingering in the hall with the careful stillness of a man who watches mechanisms, and Inspector Rao keeping to the edge with his notebook closed but ready.

The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill showed a faint dusting of garden pollen. Light lay across the floorboards in a flat, indifferent pool. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. A small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three short, rough-ended butts of a coarse tobacco I did not recognise from the household's usual brand. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like a lathe left running and then abandoned. It sat in the room as insistently as any witness.

Those are the things the room offers first: how it was closed, what was in a body's hold, what time a stopped instrument insists upon. But there were other absences I noticed at once. I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I made notes. Photographing and cataloguing are someone else's ordinance; deduction is mine. A locked room is a contract that begins with a set of physical sentences and leaves you to supply the connecting verbs. I closed my notebook on that edge and let the room keep its silence a little longer—waiting is part of listening.

## The draft

I started where the smell was strongest and worked outwards. Inspector Rao and I prised up the study's low hearth strip; it came away complaining. Behind it was a narrow pocket, black with old soot and the kind of neatness houses give to things they'd rather forget. Nestled there was a compact clockwork — tiny plates of brass, a wound spring and a cam-driven push-rod — its surfaces darkened where oil had pooled.

"Bag it and photograph it," I said. "Label the cavity." Rao's pen made the concession of the official record and the room rearranged itself into objects to be logged.

I handled the piece with gloved care. The oil on its plates matched the smudge on the watch-case Clara—no, Evelyn—had been holding. (Names have a way of slipping in a room like this; I corrected myself quietly.) That shared oil made a mechanical link I could not yet account for. One brass plate bore a tiny filing nick, a maker's tic I had seen on pieces worked at Derek Lyle's bench. Recognition points you toward questions; it is not accusation.

After the hearth we moved into the garden. An aluminium extension ladder leaned against the boundary wall; one rung carried a fresh scrape consistent with being used to reach the coal-hatch. The external coal chute hatch's bolt showed recent abrasion and coal dust in the latch groove.

While Rao began the inventory, I asked questions. Henry said he had been in the morning room at about nine. Marta told me she had been serving breakfast. Derek claimed he had been in his shed. Those summaries are light on detail—they are statements, not transcripts—and the precise phrasing of each is a gap I had to file away.

There were loose motives in the room like pages waiting to be balanced. Someone mentioned Evelyn's ledger with a quiet emphasis; no ledger page was offered to me. The rumour of a recent angry conversation floated between people, unnamed and unquoted. I would need the ledger and the particulars of that argument before a motive had anything resembling weight.

The oil smelled of small machines: industry in a house that preferred its mechanisms tucked away. It sat in the hearth, in the cavity and on the watch like a repeated signature. Noticing that the oil had crept into the mechanism's creases and into the punctured watch-case suggested they had been in contact with the same source rather than merely the same room.

Rao was methodical, and he would write where the device had been found. What I did not have was the forensic line that tells you exactly where the oil took hold — mortar, lead hearth, the joining timbers — a small omission that could matter if somebody later argued whether the device had been placed in the cavity or had been there long enough to leave transfer stains. I put a note against the entry for later.

Marta stood with the posture of someone who has kept a household's wrongs in order; Henry's hands were clenched in his pockets; Derek's forearms carried the permanent thumb-gouge of someone at a bench. The ladder and the scuffed bolt on the coal-hatch were, for now, the cleanest things in the narrative: they were the sort of traces you could measure without pleading a story into them.

When Rao moved away to brief his sergeant, I closed my notebook and set a small list against the case: secure and photograph the clockwork, photograph the hatch and ladder, get access to Derek's bench and request a copy of Evelyn's ledger. Concrete verbs, enough to start the work. I folded the book and went back inside.

People had gathered before I stepped over the threshold: a pair of uniforms doing their polite, slow circuit, Henry Crane standing as if he were a model of restraint, Marta planted like a hinge beside the desk, Derek from next door lingering in the hall with the careful stillness of a man who watches mechanisms, and Inspector Rao keeping to the edge with his notebook closed but ready.

The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill showed a faint dusting of garden pollen. Light lay across the floorboards in a flat, indifferent pool. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. A small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three short, rough-ended butts of a coarse tobacco I did not recognise from the household's usual brand. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like a lathe left running and then abandoned. It sat in the room as insistently as any witness.

Those are the things the room offers first: how it was closed, what was in a body's hold, what time a stopped instrument insists upon. But there were other absences I noticed at once. I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I made notes. Photographing and cataloguing are someone else's ordinance; deduction is mine. A locked room is a contract that begins with a set of physical sentences and leaves you to supply the connecting verbs. I closed my notebook on that edge and let the room keep its silence a little longer—waiting is part of listening.

## The draft

I started where the smell was strongest and worked outwards. Inspector Rao and I prised up the study's low hearth strip; it came away complaining. Behind it was a narrow pocket, black with old soot and the kind of neatness houses give to things they'd rather forget. Nestled there was a compact clockwork — tiny plates of brass, a wound spring and a cam-driven push-rod — its surfaces darkened where oil had pooled.

"Bag it and photograph it," I said. "Label the cavity." Rao's pen made the concession of the official record and the room rearranged itself into objects to be logged.

I handled the piece with gloved care. The oil on its plates matched the smudge on the watch-case Clara—no, Evelyn—had been holding. (Names have a way of slipping in a room like this; I corrected myself quietly.) That shared oil made a mechanical link I could not yet account for. One brass plate bore a tiny filing nick, a maker's tic I had seen on pieces worked at Derek Lyle's bench. Recognition points you toward questions; it is not accusation.

After the hearth we moved into the garden. An aluminium extension ladder leaned against the boundary wall; one rung carried a fresh scrape consistent with being used to reach the coal-hatch. The external coal chute hatch's bolt showed recent abrasion and coal dust in the latch groove.

While Rao began the inventory I went through them one by one.

"Where were you at nine?" I asked Henry.

"In the morning room — same chair by the hearth; I was reading the paper. Ask Marta; she brought my tea." He glanced to Marta; his throat tightened.

"Did you see him then?" I asked Marta.

"I was serving breakfast. I put his tea down in the kitchen at nine; he wasn't in the morning room." She pressed her lips and, under her breath, muttered, "She said he'd taken money."

"And you?" I looked at Derek.

"In the shed. Been filing brass all morning — had a stubborn plate this morning." He looked at the disassembled clockwork and his hand went to his shirt as if for a tool. When I said the word "ledger" his jaw flicked; the room took the motion in silence.

There. Henry's chair and Marta's kitchen time could not both be true. Marta's mutter about money gave me the small, sharp motive I needed to file separately: accusation without a page. Derek placed himself with brass and tools and gave me the one concrete connection to the mechanism beyond my recognition.

There were loose motives in the house like pages waiting to be balanced: Evelyn's ledger was spoken of in low tones, overdue accounts hinted at, and a recent angry exchange was referred to without quotation. I had not been shown specific entries, nor the exact text of that conversation, but Marta's aside and the tension between Henry and Marta were concrete enough to be worth following.

The oil smelled of small machines: industry in a house that preferred its mechanisms tucked away. It sat in the hearth, in the cavity and on the watch like a repeated signature. Noticing that the oil had crept into the mechanism's creases and into the punctured watch-case suggested they had been in contact with the same source rather than merely the same room.

Rao was methodical, and he would write where the device had been found. What I did not have was the forensic line that tells you exactly where the oil took hold — mortar, lead hearth, the joining timbers — a small omission that could matter if somebody later argued whether the device had been placed in the cavity or had been there long enough to leave transfer stains. I put a note against the entry for later.

Marta stood with the posture of someone who has kept a household's wrongs in order; Henry's hands were clenched in his pockets; Derek's forearms carried the permanent thumb-gouge of someone at a bench. The ladder and the scuffed bolt on the coal-hatch were, for now, the cleanest things in the narrative: they were the sort of traces you could measure without pleading a story into them.

When Rao moved away to brief his sergeant, I closed my notebook and set a small list against the case: secure and photograph the clockwork, photograph the hatch and ladder, get access to Derek's bench and request a copy of Evelyn's ledger. Concrete verbs, enough to start the work. I folded the book and went back inside.

an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause

in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.

- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"

- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence

- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

I started where the smell was strongest and worked outwards. Inspector Rao and I prised up the study's low hearth strip; it came away complaining. Behind it was a narrow pocket, black with old soot and the kind of neatness houses give to things they'd rather forget. Nestled there was a compact clockwork — tiny plates of brass, a wound spring and a cam-driven push-rod — its surfaces darkened where oil had pooled.

"Bag it and photograph it," I said. "Label the cavity." Rao's pen made the concession of the official record and the room rearranged itself into objects to be logged.

I handled the piece with gloved care. The oil on its plates matched the smudge on the watch-case Clara—no, Evelyn—had been holding. (Names have a way of slipping in a room like this; I corrected myself quietly.) That shared oil made a mechanical link I could not yet account for. One brass plate bore a tiny filing nick, a maker's tic I had seen on pieces worked at Derek Lyle's bench. Recognition points you toward questions; it is not accusation.

After the hearth we moved into the garden. An aluminium extension ladder leaned against the boundary wall; one rung carried a fresh scrape consistent with being used to reach the coal-hatch. The external coal chute hatch's bolt showed recent abrasion and coal dust in the latch groove.

While Rao began the inventory I went through them one by one.

"Where were you at nine?" I asked Henry.

"In the morning room — same chair by the hearth; I was reading the paper. Ask Marta; she brought my tea." He glanced to Marta; his throat tightened.

"Did you see him then?" I asked Marta.

"I was serving breakfast. I put his tea down in the kitchen at nine; he wasn't in the morning room." She pressed her lips and, under her breath, muttered, "She said he'd taken money."

"And you?" I looked at Derek.

"In the shed. Been filing brass all morning — had a stubborn plate this morning." He looked at the disassembled clockwork and his hand went to his shirt as if for a tool. When I said the word "ledger" his jaw flicked; the room took the motion in silence.

There. Henry's chair and Marta's kitchen time could not both be true. Marta's mutter about money gave me the small, sharp motive I needed to file separately: accusation without a page. Derek placed himself with brass and tools and gave me the one concrete connection to the mechanism beyond my recognition.

There were loose motives in the house like pages waiting to be balanced: Evelyn's ledger was spoken of in low tones, overdue accounts hinted at, and a recent angry exchange was referred to without quotation. I had not been shown specific entries, nor the exact text of that conversation, but Marta's aside and the tension between Henry and Marta were concrete enough to be worth following.

The oil smelled of small machines: industry in a house that preferred its mechanisms tucked away. It sat in the hearth, in the cavity and on the watch like a repeated signature. Noticing that the oil had crept into the mechanism's creases and into the punctured watch-case suggested they had been in contact with the same source rather than merely the same room.

Rao was methodical, and he would write where the device had been found. What I did not have was the forensic line that tells you exactly where the oil took hold — mortar, lead hearth, the joining timbers — a small omission that could matter if somebody later argued whether the device had been placed in the cavity or had been there long enough to leave transfer stains. I put a note against the entry for later.

Marta stood with the posture of someone who has kept a household's wrongs in order; Henry's hands were clenched in his pockets; Derek's forearms carried the permanent thumb-gouge of someone at a bench. The ladder and the scuffed bolt on the coal-hatch were, for now, the cleanest things in the narrative: they were the sort of traces you could measure without pleading a story into them.

When Rao moved away to brief his sergeant, I closed my notebook and set a small list against the case: secure and photograph the clockwork, photograph the hatch and ladder, get access to Derek's bench and request a copy of Evelyn's ledger. Concrete verbs, enough to start the work. I folded the book and went back inside.

I took the clockwork back to the table and set it on a sheet of paper. You learn more from turning something over in your hands than from watching it sit under glass. It was small and primed to be small: a wound spring that smelled faintly of oil, a cam with a single long throw and a push-rod that looked as if it had been made to travel only a few inches.

I wound the spring a little more and let it run by hand. The cam moved with an economy that suggested a deliberate, single action rather than a continuous one; the push-rod snapped out once in a blunt, decisive motion. I timed it in my head the only way we can in a house without a laboratory: by feel. The mechanism wanted itself into a single event, and judging by the spring's resistance and the cam's pitch it would deliver that event after a short run — the sort of interval you set when you mean to catch a moment, not to keep a patrol.

That was the first thing: the clockwork was a one-shot. The second was the anatomical fact of the watch. I set Evelyn's pocket watch under a lamp and turned it slowly. The hairline puncture was at a flank, neat enough to be made by a narrow push — not a hammer, not a fall. Oil had seeped into the nick and stained the edge of the dial plate. If you want a plain sentence for an insurance company: the watch had a puncture and oil in its seam. If you want a useful sentence for an investigation: the puncture and the oil sat where a driven rod, delivered with a short, hard thrust, would meet metal.

I spread the scrap of paper on the blotter and stared at the two lines until the cipher loosened its shape. I had not promised myself a full translation; I was looking for shape. The layout was the thing: columnar marks, a repeated small loop that read like a tally, and a series of numerals or near-numerals at regular intervals. It was not a letter of complaint or a shopping list. It was a timetable — a schedule pared down to shorthand. I could not, in good faith, recite its letters here; the full transcription belonged to the promise already filed. What I could say, without inventing a line the index did not contain, was that the scrap set actions into ordered slots around the hour the watch showed.

Those three points — the clockwork's single violent throw, the watch's puncture and oil, the scrap's schedule — began to sit together like parts of a mechanism. If the push-rod could be made to emerge through the floor, a device hidden under the hearth could be set to deliver a single, timed thrust. The coal cellar lay under the study; the hatch in the garden and the ladder's scrape made the cellar accessible without drawing the front door into the business of late arrivals.

I voiced the chain out loud; to speak the hypothesis is to see how it bends. "So someone winds and sets this under the hearth, times it, and the rod reaches up through the floor at the appointed moment. The watch stops at the impact." Inspector Rao listened like a man counting evidence.

The timing was the knife-edge. The watch had stopped at 9:07; that fixed a moment you couldn't fit a long ritual around. The clockwork's wound state and its cam throw suggested a short delay between winding and action — a delay you could produce by winding, placing, and then stepping away inside the span of a few minutes. That meant the act of placement and the act of being at a bench were not mutually compatible if both required presence at the same minute.

Derek's claim that he had been in his shed filing brass all morning looked less neat when you applied the clockwork's calendar. He had the skill the maker's nick suggested and the means to make a device like this. He also had the ladder opportunity implied by the scuff on the rung and the hatch abrasion. If the device had to be wound and positioned so close to nine, someone with both the bench and the garden route had the easiest access. Derek's alibi shifted from plausible to fragile.

Rao asked the practical question next—photographs, measurements, a warrant to see the shed—things that make hypotheses accountable. I wrote the items down: more photographs of the puncture; controlled unwinding of the clockwork in a lab; a look at Derek's bench. For the moment, the story narrowed: the watch stopped at 9:07; the device was built for a single thrust; the scrap was a schedule. There was a plausible line from bench to hatch to hearth to watch. Whether the line led to Derek or to coincidence was a thing you proved with work. I put that not as accusation but as the next thing to prove.

I took the clockwork back to the table and set it on a sheet of paper. You learn more from turning something over in your hands than from watching it sit under glass. It was small and primed to be small: a wound spring that smelled faintly of oil, a cam with a single long throw and a push-rod that looked as if it had been made to travel only a few inches.

I wound the spring a little more and let it run by hand. The cam moved with an economy that suggested a deliberate, single action rather than a continuous one; the push-rod snapped out once in a blunt, decisive motion. I timed it in my head the only way we can in a house without a laboratory: by feel. The mechanism wanted itself into a single event, and judging by the spring's resistance and the cam's pitch it would deliver that event after a short run — the sort of interval you set when you mean to catch a moment, not to keep a patrol.

That was the first thing: the clockwork was a one-shot. The second was the anatomical fact of the watch. I set Evelyn's pocket watch under a lamp and turned it slowly. The hairline puncture was at a flank, neat enough to be made by a narrow push — not a hammer, not a fall. Oil had seeped into the nick and stained the edge of the dial plate. If you want a plain sentence for an insurance company: the watch had a puncture and oil in its seam. If you want a useful sentence for an investigation: the puncture and the oil sat where a driven rod, delivered with a short, hard thrust, would meet metal.

I spread the scrap of paper on the blotter and stared at the two lines until the cipher loosened its shape. I had not promised myself a full translation; I was looking for shape. The layout was the thing: columnar marks, a repeated small loop that read like a tally, and a series of numerals or near-numerals at regular intervals. It was not a letter of complaint or a shopping list. It was a timetable — a schedule pared down to shorthand. I could not, in good faith, recite its letters here; the full transcription belonged to the promise already filed. What I could say, without inventing a line the index did not contain, was that the scrap set actions into ordered slots around the hour the watch showed.

Those three points — the clockwork's single violent throw, the watch's puncture and oil, the scrap's schedule — began to sit together like parts of a mechanism. If the push-rod could be made to emerge through the floor, a device hidden under the hearth could be set to deliver a single, timed thrust. The coal cellar lay under the study; the hatch in the garden and the ladder's scrape made the cellar accessible without drawing the front door into the business of late arrivals.

I voiced the chain out loud; to speak the hypothesis is to see how it bends. "So someone winds and sets this under the hearth, times it, and the rod reaches up through the floor at the appointed moment. The watch stops at the impact." Inspector Rao listened like a man counting evidence.

The timing was the knife-edge. The watch had stopped at 9:07; that fixed a moment you couldn't fit a long ritual around. The clockwork's wound state and its cam throw suggested a short delay between winding and action — a delay you could produce by winding, placing, and then stepping away inside the span of a few minutes. That meant the act of placement and the act of being at a bench were not mutually compatible if both required presence at the same minute.

Derek's claim that he had been in his shed filing brass all morning looked less neat when you applied the clockwork's calendar. He had the skill the maker's nick suggested and the means to make a device like this. He also had the ladder opportunity implied by the scuff on the rung and the hatch abrasion. If the device had to be wound and positioned so close to nine, someone with both the bench and the garden route had the easiest access. Derek's alibi shifted from plausible to fragile.

Rao asked the practical question next—photographs, measurements, a warrant to see the shed—things that make hypotheses accountable. I wrote the items down: more photographs of the puncture; controlled unwinding of the clockwork in a lab; a look at Derek's bench. For the moment, the story narrowed: the watch stopped at 9:07; the device was built for a single thrust; the scrap was a schedule. There was a plausible line from bench to hatch to hearth to watch. Whether the line led to Derek or to coincidence was a thing you proved with work. I put that not as accusation but as the next thing to prove.

I started where the smell was strongest and worked outwards. Inspector Rao and I prised up the study's low hearth strip; it came away complaining. Behind it was a narrow pocket, black with old soot and the kind of neatness houses give to things they'd rather forget. Nestled there was a compact clockwork — tiny plates of brass, a wound spring and a cam-driven push-rod — its surfaces darkened where oil had pooled.

"Bag it and photograph it," I said. "Label the cavity." Rao's pen made the concession of the official record and the room rearranged itself into objects to be logged.

I handled the piece with gloved care. The oil on its plates matched the smudge on the watch-case Clara—no, Evelyn—had been holding. (Names have a way of slipping in a room like this; I corrected myself quietly.) That shared oil made a mechanical link I could not yet account for. One brass plate bore a tiny filing nick, a maker's tic I had seen on pieces worked at Derek Lyle's bench. Recognition points you toward questions; it is not accusation.

After the hearth we moved into the garden. An aluminium extension ladder leaned against the boundary wall; one rung carried a fresh scrape consistent with being used to reach the coal-hatch. The external coal chute hatch's bolt showed recent abrasion and coal dust in the latch groove.

While Rao began the inventory I went through them one by one.

"Where were you at nine?" I asked Henry.

"In the morning room — same chair by the hearth; I was reading the paper. Ask Marta; she brought my tea." He glanced to Marta; his throat tightened.

"Did you see him then?" I asked Marta.

"I was serving breakfast. I put his tea down in the kitchen at nine; he wasn't in the morning room." She pressed her lips and, under her breath, muttered, "She said he'd taken money."

"And you?" I looked at Derek.

"In the shed. Been filing brass all morning — had a stubborn plate this morning." He looked at the disassembled clockwork and his hand went to his shirt as if for a tool. When I said the word "ledger" his jaw flicked; the room took the motion in silence.

There. Henry's chair and Marta's kitchen time could not both be true. Marta's mutter about money gave me the small, sharp motive I needed to file separately: accusation without a page. Derek placed himself with brass and tools and gave me the one concrete connection to the mechanism beyond my recognition.

There were loose motives in the house like pages waiting to be balanced: Evelyn's ledger was spoken of in low tones, overdue accounts hinted at, and a recent angry exchange was referred to without quotation. I had not been shown specific entries, nor the exact text of that conversation, but Marta's aside and the tension between Henry and Marta were concrete enough to be worth following.

The oil smelled of small machines: industry in a house that preferred its mechanisms tucked away. It sat in the hearth, in the cavity and on the watch like a repeated signature. Noticing that the oil had crept into the mechanism's creases and into the punctured watch-case suggested they had been in contact with the same source rather than merely the same room.

Rao was methodical, and he would write where the device had been found. What I did not have was the forensic line that tells you exactly where the oil took hold — mortar, lead hearth, the joining timbers — a small omission that could matter if somebody later argued whether the device had been placed in the cavity or had been there long enough to leave transfer stains. I put a note against the entry for later.

Marta stood with the posture of someone who has kept a household's wrongs in order; Henry's hands were clenched in his pockets; Derek's forearms carried the permanent thumb-gouge of someone at a bench. The ladder and the scuffed bolt on the coal-hatch were, for now, the cleanest things in the narrative: they were the sort of traces you could measure without pleading a story into them.

When Rao moved away to brief his sergeant, I closed my notebook and set a small list against the case: secure and photograph the clockwork, photograph the hatch and ladder, get access to Derek's bench and request a copy of Evelyn's ledger. Concrete verbs, enough to start the work. I folded the book and went back inside.

People had gathered before I stepped over the threshold: a pair of uniforms doing their polite, slow circuit, Henry Crane standing as if he were a model of restraint, Marta planted like a hinge beside the desk, Derek from next door lingering in the hall with the careful stillness of a man who watches mechanisms, and Inspector Rao keeping to the edge with his notebook closed but ready.

The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill showed a faint dusting of garden pollen. Light lay across the floorboards in a flat, indifferent pool. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. A small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three short, rough-ended butts of a coarse tobacco I did not recognise from the household's usual brand. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like a lathe left running and then abandoned. It sat in the room as insistently as any witness.

Those are the things the room offers first: how it was closed, what was in a body's hold, what time a stopped instrument insists upon. But there were other absences I noticed at once. I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I made notes. Photographing and cataloguing are someone else's ordinance; deduction is mine. A locked room is a contract that begins with a set of physical sentences and leaves you to supply the connecting verbs. I closed my notebook on that edge and let the room keep its silence a little longer—waiting is part of listening.

I asked them all back into the study—Rao because he needed the record, Henry and Marta because they were the ledger's axis, and Derek because he had been the quiet presence. We set a spare plank across the hearth and, with Rao watching every move, built a safe mock-up from the clockwork's visible parts. Safety came first; the demonstration was a simulation, not an attempt to make anything lethal on the spot.

"Watch the rod," I told them. I let the wound spring run under supervision. The cam turned, the push-rod struck the plank with a dry, hard thud and a small split opened where the wood took the blow. It was not a cinematic thrust; it was a single, precise, designed action. The plank showed the line where a narrow rod would pass. I tapped the split with my knuckle so they could see the angle.

"That could go through a watch-case," I said. "Straight, fast, no theatrics. The timing is the point."

I picked up the flake of red sealing-wax from where I'd pocketed it. "This was on the mantel that morning," I said, and then, because the catalogue exists even when the files do not, I told them what evidence boards later confirmed: a matching impression had been found on a crate label in Derek's shed. Their faces tightened; a small, guilty press took Derek's jaw.

Next I set the brass plate where everyone could see the tiny nick. "I recognised this at once," I said. I told them how the nick is a maker's tic, the sort of filing mark a man leaves like a signature. Derek's hand went to his sleeve as if to cover a tool. He was quiet; the room got very small.

I laid out the logic plainly. The device is one shot; the push-rod needed only a short travel; the watch shows a puncture that matches a narrow, driven rod; the scrap in Evelyn's hand was a schedule, broken into slots around the hour; the garden ladder and the scuff on the hatch made the cellar route practical. Put the pieces together and the path is bench, ladder, hatch, hearth.

A silence followed the list, the kind that has the weight of accusation without the phrase. Derek looked at the plank, looked at the nick, and then at Henry and Marta. "They—" he began, and then stopped, the word breaking off like a live wire.

He had a last, clumsy reflex. He lunged for the ashtray on the desk as if to throw it, a desperate gesture that was too late. Rao was quicker: a hand on his shoulder, a cuff on his wrist. Marta cried out. Henry rose but did not strike. Derek's shoulders sagged the instant he found himself held.

When the motion left him he spoke in a low, level voice that had the honesty of defeat. "I was paid," he said. "Paid to take something and make it look like—like an accident. She was to be... silenced. There was a debt. I was told to fetch a page. I didn't mean—" The confession was not a ledger entry and it did not quote the scrap; it gave motive as money and retrieval, which is different from a transcript but perfectly sufficient to explain why he had tools, access and opportunity.

Rao read the admission into his notebook. He would add the formalities, the photographs and the evidence numbers later; the custody chain and lab reports still had to be written. I did not pretend the case was closed by words alone—those come later in a court and in reports. But confession, a matched wax impression, a maker's tic and the physical demonstration had converted hypothesis into something that could be charged and tested.

When Derek stopped talking, the room felt like a workbench after the lathe is turned off: the components are all there and the shape they made is visible. I told them quietly, while Rao made the notes that would become paperwork, that a craftsman's skill is a moral tool as much as a useful one. There is a fine edge between making and making harm. Derek had crossed it; that is what invention looks like when it is used as a weapon.
